Obsessive-Compulsive and Related Disorders

obsessions and compulsions · insight · related disorders · ERP and SSRIsDoes the repeated act neutralize an unwanted thought?

Practice
  1. 28-year-old man has unwanted images of pushing strangers onto train tracks Horrified, he avoids platforms and silently repeats a prayer to cancel each image No hallucinations; the rituals take two hours a day → Start an SSRI → Ego-dystonic violent images cancelled by a mental ritual for over an hour a day are OCD; an SSRI with ERP is first line, antipsychotics only augment an SSRI, and anxiolytics do not treat obsessions and compulsions
  2. 41-year-old accountant keeps missing deadlines because she redoes reports until every detail is perfect She insists coworkers follow her lists and will not delegate She sees her standards as correct and has no intrusive thoughts or rituals → Obsessive-compulsive personality disorder → Pervasive perfectionism and control that she sees as correct, with no obsessions or compulsions, is OCPD; OCD is ego-dystonic
  3. 67-year-old man cannot throw away old newspapers and mail, even items of no value Stacks fill his kitchen and hallway, so he cannot cook, and a fall hazard is noted He feels distress at the idea of discarding anything → Hoarding disorder → Difficulty discarding possessions regardless of their value, with clutter that makes living areas unusable or unsafe, is hoarding disorder, treated first with CBT
  4. 24-year-old woman with OCD started sertraline at a low dose 3 weeks ago Her checking rituals have eased slightly; she has no adverse effects She asks whether the drug is failing and wants to try something else → Increase the sertraline dose and continue the trial → OCD often needs a higher SSRI dose than depression, and a trial is judged only after 8 to 12 weeks, 4 to 6 of them at the top tolerated dose
  5. Three weeks after delivery, a 30-year-old woman has repeated images of drowning her baby in the bath She knows the images are senseless, avoids bathing the infant, and checks on her often at night No hallucinations or unusual beliefs → Obsessive-compulsive disorder → After delivery, OCD commonly takes the form of fears of contaminating or harming the baby; she knows the thoughts are irrational, unlike a patient with psychosis
  6. 35-year-old man with severe contamination fears has had full trials of fluoxetine and sertraline Each reached the highest tolerated dose for 12 weeks, alongside ERP He still washes his hands for 3 hours a day → Clomipramine → After adequate trials of at least two SSRIs, clomipramine, a strongly serotonergic tricyclic, is the second-line option; antipsychotics only augment an SSRI, and anxiolytics do not treat OCD
  7. 19-year-old man is convinced his nose is crooked, though others see nothing wrong He checks mirrors for hours, has seen three plastic surgeons, and skips class He has no other repeated rituals or intrusive thoughts → Body dysmorphic disorder → Preoccupation with an imagined defect in appearance, with mirror checking and repeated cosmetic visits, is body dysmorphic disorder; it is treated with SSRIs and/or CBT
Pairs with Tics and Tic Disorders: tic-related OCD and exposure and response prevention. Hair Loss in a Child: trichotillomania. Panic Disorder and Other Anxiety: generalized anxiety disorder. SSRI Adverse Effects: the first-line drugs.
Transferable rule

If a repeated act neutralizes an unwanted thought, it is a compulsion: treat with ERP and an SSRI. If the patient sees the rigid trait as right, think of OCPD.
